Hi Samir — following up with the concrete explainer Marissa promised. Pasting the short version here and attaching a worked example (tokens_pricing_example.pdf) + a sample traffic CSV you can fill in.

Short explainer
- Token vs character: A token is roughly 3–4 characters on average for English, but it varies by language and content. Characters are not a billing unit; they're just an approximation folks sometimes use.
- Requests vs tokens: A request = one API call. Each request consumes input tokens (your prompt) + output tokens (model completion). Example: a 200-char prompt might be ~50 tokens; a 1500-char generated summary might be ~375 tokens. That request costs tokens = prompt_tokens + completion_tokens.
- Billing: Redwood bills for tokens (input + output). So request_count * avg_tokens_per_request = billed_tokens.
- Caching and billed tokens: prompt-prefix caching and KV cache reduce billed tokens when requests are identical or share cached prefixes. Important distinctions:
  * Prompt caching: if many requests reuse the same leading prompt (e.g., standard system prompt + patient demographics), we can store the prefix so the model only computes and bills for the varying suffix and the output. That lowers billed input tokens for cached traffic.
  * KV cache (for long chats): reusing the KV cache can avoid re-sending the full conversation history on repeated requests to the same session, reducing billed input tokens during that session until the cache is invalidated.
  * Note: Caching helps billed tokens when the payloads match the cache policy. If your requests are all unique, caching won't reduce billed tokens.

Worked example (from attachment) — approximate numbers for illustration
- Model A (high-quality generation): list price $10 per 1M tokens.
- Baseline request: 150 tokens input + 350 tokens output = 500 tokens/request.
- If you have 20k requests/month (all similar), billed tokens = 20k * 500 = 10M tokens => cost ~ $100 (at $10/1M tokens that's $100 for 10M tokens — note: example numbers simplified).

Important: unit economics depend heavily on avg tokens/request and cache hit rate. If you can cache 50% of the prompt tokens, you can see a material reduction in billed tokens.
